rows.description: A young adult researches a project for weeks, refining an outline that is never good enough to begin. Preparing feels productive but is a way of postponing the risk of being judged.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: Deadlines pass without a submission or a job application because nothing seems ready. Doing nothing feels safer than doing something imperfect, though it guarantees the failure the person fears.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A teacher or friend sees strong ability going unused and the person turning down chances. Praising effort and progress, not only results, and showing one's own flawed drafts helps loosen the grip.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A teacher notes a student who never turns in drafts and cries over a small mark. Praising the effort, letting the student see teachers' own mistakes and allowing messy first tries reduce the fear.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: Seeing peers ship imperfect work and succeed brings envy and confusion, along with shame at being stuck. The person starts to see that the rules they held were their own, not the world's.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22
related mind states: shame, confusion, envy

rows.description: The person sets a time limit, sends a rough draft to a trusted person and notes that nothing terrible happened. Small controlled exposure to imperfection slowly retrains the fear response.
graph_context: previous stage: The crash of comparison
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: Standards remain but are held lightly, valuing learning over flawlessness and separating self-worth from output. The person finishes things, accepts feedback and, if fear stays intense, seeks a counsellor.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A child begins tabla, chess or coding and sees quick early gains. Everything is new and every step is a win, so motivation is easy and expectations quietly rise.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Stage 2: The gap between taste and ability [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager learning guitar or maths hears what good sounds like and sees their own work fall short. The frustration comes from having good taste before skill, and it is a sign of growth, not lack of talent.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: Weeks of practice show no visible progress and the person suspects they have hit their limit. Improvement is happening under the surface, but the mind reads no visible change as no change.
graph_context: previous stage: The gap between taste and ability
this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
